eructation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin ērūctātiōnem, accusative of ērūctātiō (“a belching forth, burp”), from ērūctāre (“to belch, burp”). Compare Middle English eructuacioun (“belching, burp”), borrowed from the same root.

s.d: (of volcanoes) pouring out fumes or lava (or a deposit so formed)
a reflex that expels gas noisily from the stomach through the mouth
(uncountable) The act of belching, of expelling gas from the stomach through the mouth.
x: His eyes were as restless as his limbs, and seemed ever to be seeking for something upon which they could definitely alight, and not finding it. He performed eructations with the disarming naturalness of a baby.
"Move along, you coxcomb," Ignatius belched, the gassy eructations echoing between the walls of the alley.

s.d: (uncountable) An erumpent blast of gas, wind, or other matter ejected from the depths of the earth.

erudite.e: From Latin ērudītus, participle of ērudiō (“educate, train”), from e- (“out of”) + rudis (“rude, unskilled”). Doublet of erudit.

s.d: a learned or scholarly person
having or showing profound knowledge
x: a learned jurist
an erudite professor

s.d: Learned, scholarly, with emphasis on knowledge gained from books.
x: The professor gave an erudite lecture that impressed everyone in the audience.
His erudite knowledge of ancient history made him a sought-after speaker.

eruditely.e:
Etymology tree
English erudite
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English eruditely
From erudite + -ly.

s.d: with erudition; in an erudite manner
x: he talked eruditely about Indian mythology

s.d: In a learned or scholarly manner.
profound scholarly knowledge
(uncountable) erudition

erudition.e: First attested in the 15th Century. From Middle French érudition, from Latin eruditio (“an instructing, learning, erudition”), from erudire (“to instruct, educate, cultivate”, literally “free from rudeness”), from e (“out”) + rudis (“rude”). By surface analysis, erudite + -ion.

s.d: profound scholarly knowledge
(uncountable) Profound knowledge acquired from learning and scholarship.
x: As a philosopher he was superior to Lenin in all respects: erudition, knowledge of his subject, independence of thought, and skill in formulating problems.

s.d: (uncountable) The refinement, polish and knowledge that education confers.

erupt.e: From Latin eruptus, past participle of ērumpō (“to break out (of), to burst out (from)”), from e (“out”) + rumpō (“to break”).

s.d: start abruptly
x: After 1989, peace broke out in the former East Bloc

s.d: erupt or intensify suddenly
x: Unrest erupted in the country
Tempers flared at the meeting

s.d: start to burn or burst into flames
x: Marsh gases ignited suddenly
The oily rags combusted spontaneously

s.d: break out
x: The tooth erupted and had to be extracted

s.d: become active and spew forth lava and rocks
x: Vesuvius erupts once in a while

s.d: force out or release suddenly and often violently something pent up
x: break into tears
erupt in anger

s.d: appear on the skin
x: A rash erupted on her arms after she had touched the exotic plant

s.d: become raw or open
x: He broke out in hives
My skin breaks out when I eat strawberries

s.d: To eject something violently (such as lava or water, as from a volcano or geyser).
x: The volcano erupted, spewing lava across a wide area.

s.d: (figuratively) To spontaneously release pressure or tension.
x: The crowd erupted in anger.
The whole table erupted in laughter.

s.d: (Of birds, insects, etc.) To suddenly appear in a certain region in large numbers.
x: After particularly good seasons, flocks "erupt" from their breeding grounds and appear in reed beds where they have not been seen for years, if ever.

eruption.e: From Middle French éruption, from Latin eruptio.

s.d: the sudden occurrence of a violent discharge of steam and volcanic material
symptom consisting of a breaking out and becoming visible
(of volcanoes) pouring out fumes or lava (or a deposit so formed)
a sudden violent spontaneous occurrence (usually of some undesirable condition)
x: the outbreak of hostilities

s.d: a sudden very loud noise
the emergence of a tooth as it breaks through the gum
(uncountable) A violent ejection, such as the spurting out of lava from a volcano.
x: a volcanic eruption

s.d: (uncountable) A sudden release of pressure or tension.
x: There was an eruption of joy at the final whistle.

s.d: (uncountable) An utterance, especially a sudden one; an ejaculation.
(uncountable) An infection of the skin resulting in a rash or blemishing.

eruptive.e: From French éruptif. By surface analysis, erupt + -ive.

s.d: An eruptive rock, one produced by eruption.
producing or characterized by eruptions
x: an eruptive disease

s.d: produced by the action of fire or intense heat
x: rocks formed by igneous agents

s.d: actively spewing out lava
x: a geyser is an intermittently eruptive hot spring

s.d: That erupts or bursts forth.
x: ’Tis liſtening fear, and dumb amazement all: / When to the ſtartled eye the ſudden glance / Appears far ſouth, eruptive thro’ the cloud; […]

s.d: Accompanied by eruptions.
x: an eruptive fever

s.d: Produced by eruption.
x: eruptive rocks, such as the igneous or volcanic
The region is further diversified by short ranges of eruptive mountains.

s.d: rod-shaped motile bacteria that attack plants

eryngo.e: Ultimately from Latin ēryngion, from Ancient Greek ἠρύγγιον (ērúngion), from ἤρυγγος (ḗrungos).

s.d: any plant of the genus Eryngium
(obsolete, uncountable) The root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly candied and taken as confectionery and held to have aphrodisiac properties.
x: Let the skie raine Potatoes: let it thunder, to the tune of Greene-ſleeues, haile-kiſſing Comfits, and ſnovv Eringoes: […]

erysipelas.e: From Middle English erisipila, borrowed from Latin erysipelas, from Ancient Greek ἐρῠσῐ́πελᾰς (erŭsĭ́pelăs), probably related to ἐρῠθρός (erŭthrós, “red”) and πέλμᾰ (pélmă, “the sole of a foot”).

s.d: an acute streptococcal infection characterized by deep-red inflammation of the skin and mucous membranes

(uncountable) An acute, sometimes recurrent febrile disease caused by infection of a hemolytic streptococcus, associated with intense edematous local inflammation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, and marked by large raised red patches on the skin.
x: The symptoms gradually improved until, on the fifth day from her delivery, I was pleased to find the erysipelas rapidly defervescing, the lochia natural, no subinvolution of the uterus, nor abdominal tenderness.

erythema.e: From New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”)..

s.d: abnormal redness of the skin resulting from dilation of blood vessels (as in sunburn or inflammation)
(uncountable) Abnormal redness and inflammation of the skin, due to vasodilation.
(uncountable) Skin redness from sunburn or chemical irritation
a red rash caused by hypersensitivity to a drug or disease or other allergen
skin condition characterized by tender red nodules on the shins and legs
(uncountable) An inflammatory condition characterised by inflammation of the fat cells under the skin, resulting in tender red nodules that are usually seen on both shins.
an inflammatory complication of leprosy that results in painful skin lesions on the arms and legs and face
redness of the skin caused by exposure to the rays of the sun

erythematous.e: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: erythemato- + -ous.

s.d: relating to or characterized by erythema
Of or pertaining to erythema.
any of various shrubs or shrubby trees of the genus Erythrina having trifoliate leaves and racemes of scarlet to coral red flowers and black seeds; cultivated as an ornamental
Any of the genus Erythrina of leguminous flowering plants; a coral tree.

s.d: a reddish mineral consisting of hydrated cobalt arsenate in monoclinic crystalline form and used in coloring glass; usually found in veins bearing cobalt and arsenic
(uncountable) Red cobalt, a secondary hydrated arsenate of cobalt minerals with the formula (Co₃(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O).
a nucleated cell in bone marrow from which red blood cells develop

erythroblastosis.e:
Etymology tree
English erythroblast
Ancient Greek -τῐς (-tĭs)
Ancient Greek -σῐς (-sĭs)
Ancient Greek -ωσις (-ōsis)bor.
New Latin -ōsislbor.
English -osis
English erythroblastosis
From erythroblast + -osis.

s.d: a blood disease characterized by the abnormal presence of erythroblasts in the blood
(uncountable) A medical condition in which erythroblasts are abnormally found in the blood

severe anemia in newborn babies; the result of Rh incompatibility between maternal and fetal blood; typically occurs when the child of an Rh-negative mother inherits Rh-positive blood from the father; can be diagnosed before birth by amniocentesis
(uncountable) A medical condition where an Rh negative mother's antibodies attack the red blood cells of an Rh positive fetus.

erythrocyte.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-
Proto-Indo-European *-rós
Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós
Proto-Hellenic *erutʰrós
Ancient Greek ἐρῠθρός (erŭthrós)der.
English erythro-
Ancient Greek κῠ́τος (kŭ́tos)der.
Latin cytader.
English -cyte
English erythrocyte
From erythro- (“red”) + -cyte (“cell”), referring to the red color of hemoglobin when oxygen is bound to it.

s.d: a mature blood cell that contains hemoglobin to carry oxygen to the bodily tissues; a biconcave disc that has no nucleus

A hemoglobin-containing cell, especially as found in humans but more generally present in the blood of most vertebrates, that is involved with the transport of oxygen; such cells are usually anucleate in humans and many other animals.
x: The want of success of these names may be attributed to their awkwardness in sound or sense; "erythrocyte" seems the best of them, but is unfortunately four-syllabled.
Granular, basic, or punctate degeneration of the erythrocyte is a condition in which this cell presents fine or coarse granules that have an affinity for basic stains.

s.d: the rate at which red blood cells settle out in a tube of blood under standardized conditions; a high rate usually indicates the presence of inflammation

The rate (usually expressed in millimeters per hour) at which red blood cells precipitate in a vertical tube over a period of one hour, often determined as a screening test for the presence of inflammation.
any substance that can cause lysis (destruction) of erythrocytes (red blood cells) and the release of their hemoglobin
any skin disorder involving abnormal redness
(uncountable) An inflammatory skin disease with erythema and scaling that affects nearly the entire cutaneous surface.
Synonym of normoblast.
relating to erythrocytes
Having a red colour; reddish
Of or pertaining to the erythrocytes, especially to their development
any substance that can cause lysis (destruction) of erythrocytes (red blood cells) and the release of their hemoglobin

erythromycin.e:
Etymology tree
English (Streptomyces) erythr(eus)
Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der.
Latin -o-bor.
English -o-
English -mycin
English erythromycin
From (Streptomyces) erythr(eus) + -o- + -mycin (“antibiotic from a Streptomyces strain”).

s.d: an antibiotic (trade name Erythrocin or E-Mycin or Ethril or Ilosone or Pediamycin) obtained from the actinomycete Streptomyces erythreus; effective against many Gram-positive bacteria and some Gram-negative
(uncountable) An antibiotic similar to penicillin, used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.

(uncountable) A broad-spectrum macrolide antibiotic C₃₇H₆₇NO₁₃ produced by an actinomycete Saccharopolyspora erythraea (formerly Streptomyces erythreus) and similar in its effects to penicillin, administered orally or topically in the treatment of infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria.
the process of producing red blood cells by the stem cells in the bone marrow

From erythropoiesis + -ic.

s.d: of or relating to the formation of red blood cells
Of or pertaining to erythropoiesis.

erythropoietin.e: From Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”) and ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker”) and -in.

s.d: a glycoprotein secreted by the kidneys that stimulates the production of red blood cells
A glycoprotein hormone that functions as a cytokine for erythrocyte precursors in bone marrow.
x: Exogenous administration of erythropoietin can, theoretically, improve endurance exercise performance in the same way as conventional blood doping procedures.
